LGAM Business Area: Planning & Development

Planning Policy

The technical architecture required to gather spatial evidence, engage citizens at scale, and formulate the statutory Local Plan.

Creating a Local Plan is a multi-year, data-intensive endeavor. Unlike the transactional nature of Development Management, Planning Policy architecture focuses on big data analytics, geospatial modeling (e.g., finding land suitable for housing), and mass citizen engagement platforms designed to capture sentiment rather than just simple form inputs.

Details of the policy making process can be found at on the create and update your local plan webpages.

The LGAM technology stack

Delivering a Local Plan requires orchestrating analytical and engagement capabilities.

LGAM Layer LGAM Element Context in Planning Policy
Capabilities Workflow Making a local plan is a multi-year project which needs clear management and communication between policy officers working on the team.
Capabilities Forms A call for sites is a key aspect of the process, and is best done by encouraging structured and geospatial data submissions.
Business Areas Democratic services Plan-making requires regular formal and informal engagement with council members to progress.
Corporate Areas Geographical Plan-making requires the production of maps to describe various aspects of the plan, including evidence, where policies are in effect and as part of the site selection process.
Council Interfaces Websites
(Engagement) 		Interactive, map-based consultation platforms allowing citizens to drop pins and leave sentiment-driven feedback on proposed zoning changes during plan consultations.
Council Interfaces Websites
(Examination library and timetable) 		Plan-making authorities are required to publish timetables for their plan-making process and make a publicly accessible examination library of plan documents.
Integration API management and gateways Once the Plan is adopted, exposing the spatial policies as "Rules-as-code" APIs to be consumed directly by the Development Management forms engines.
Security Identity and access management (IAM) If a joint local plan is being made then employees from a range of local authority bodies will need to access and collaborate in the same workspaces.
Data and Information Geospatial data Spatial modelling to conduct Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA), overlaying flood zones, transport nodes, and conservation areas to identify viable development sites.
Data and Information Data storage and warehousing Aggregating ONS demographic data, historic housing delivery rates, and economic models into a central repository to form the "evidence base".
Data and Information Data catalogue & metadata management Keeping a clear track of plan and evidence document versions is key for compliant plan-making.

Business process

This section outlines the process of building the Local Plan. Expand each phase to compare the legacy architectural baseline against modern, data-driven target states.

1 Scoping and early participation

  • Business Process
  • Anti-patterns
  • Target Architecture

The process: Plan-making teams must run a scoping consultation and invite feedback throughout the plan-making process. They also need to set up project management practices.

Required LGAM Taxonomy Nodes:

Websites Workflow
Anti-pattern: Plan-making without tracking

A plan-making process which uses individual documents and fragmented information means manual work is required to find and access key information, as well as to provide transparency on the plan-making process to stakeholders.

Best Practice: Plan-making workflow tool

By using a dedicated tool for plan-making, documents, activities and audit logs can be held in one place. It removes the manual burden of tracking progress and supports transparency with key stakeholders.

Real-world impact
  • Reduced work to provide updates to stakeholders

    Fewer officers spend time writing reports and preparing summaries of progress.

2 Evidence base and site selection

  • Business Process
  • Anti-patterns
  • Target Architecture

The process: Policy officers must gather massive amounts of demographic, environmental, and economic data. They model this data to predict future housing needs and identify physical plots of land suitable for development (the Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment - SHLAA).

Required LGAM Taxonomy Nodes:

Geospatial data Data warehousing Business intelligence
Anti-pattern: Manual desktop spatial clicks

Conducting complex site allocation through undocumented, manual operations within desktop GIS software. The analyst manually intersects layers (e.g., "Remove flood zones, add brownfield"). If the underlying flood data updates next week, the entire manual clicking process must be repeated, and errors are untraceable.

Best Practice: Reproducible Analytical Pipelines (RAP)

Target architectures treat the Local Plan evidence base as code. Data scientists use languages like Python/R or enterprise ETL tools to create documented, version-controlled pipelines. These scripts automatically pull live data from the Corporate Data Lake and OS APIs, execute the spatial math (Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis), and output the results dynamically.

Real-world impact
  • Legal Defensibility

    When developers challenge the Local Plan at Examination, the council can demonstrably prove the exact mathematical weighting and data lineage used to allocate a specific site, removing human bias.

  • Iterative Efficiency

    If the housing target changes by 5%, the policy team simply updates one variable in the script and reruns the entire spatial model in minutes, rather than spending weeks manually re-drawing maps.

3 Consultation

  • Business Process
  • Anti-patterns
  • Target Architecture

The process: The council must consult the public on the draft plan. Citizens, developers, and statutory bodies review proposed zoning changes and provide feedback, generating thousands of responses that must be logged, categorized, and addressed.

Required LGAM Taxonomy Nodes:

Websites (Consultation) Data pipelines
Anti-pattern: The PDF and Inbox

Publishing the draft Local Plan as a massive, 300-page static PDF on the council website and asking citizens to email their feedback to a generic inbox. This creates a data-sorting nightmare for officers, who must manually read, categorize, and copy-paste thousands of unstructured emails into a spreadsheet.

Best Practice: Geospatial Engagement Platforms

Modern planning policy uses dedicated engagement platforms (e.g., Commonplace, Citizen Space). The plan is presented as an interactive web map. Citizens click on specific zones to leave feedback. The platform immediately forces the feedback into structured JSON, attaching exact geographic coordinates and categorizing sentiment before the data ever reaches the policy team.

Real-world impact
  • Democratic Reach

    Significantly increases public participation by lowering the barrier to entry (from reading a 300-page PDF to interacting with a mobile-friendly map).

  • Administrative Savings

    Eliminates hundreds of hours of manual administrative sorting. Sentiment dashboards allow officers to instantly see the primary areas of contention across the borough.

4 Gateways and examination

  • Business Process
  • Anti-patterns
  • Target Architecture

The process: Policy teams need to share their work in progress and complete plans at formal checkpoints with inspectors from the Planning Inspectorate (PINS), who need to be able to interrogate and comment on the content easily. The information needs to be shared publicly to give all stakeholders visibility of progress at these key points.

Required LGAM Taxonomy Nodes:

Data storage and warehousing Websites API gateways
Anti-pattern: Manual export and import of plan-making information

Currently plan-making teams spend a lot of time preparing document stores by sifting through internal repositories and then publishing them on their council websites. These documents aren't editable in a shared way by inspectors, so comments and recommendations are made in separate documents and then applied manually by officers afterwards, duplicating effort and increasing the risk of error.

Best Practice: Integrated inspector checkpoints

By sharing plan-making information in a structured way, inspectors spend less time reviewing and connecting information across different documents. They can also annotate and mark up the source data, which can easily be fed back into the local authority's system, reducing the laborious task of matching up modifications with changes to the plan.

Real-world impact
  • Faster inspections

    Inspectors' workflow is supported by showing the links made during policy-making.

  • Less manual editing

    Officers can see modifications against the relevant policy, making editing and tracking changes less manual.

5 Adoption and publication

  • Business Process
  • Anti-patterns
  • Target Architecture

The process: Following Examination by the Planning Inspectorate, the Local Plan is officially adopted. This plan is now the legal framework that Development Management officers must use to assess incoming planning applications.

Required LGAM Taxonomy Nodes:

API management Event-driven integration
Anti-pattern: The Disconnected Truth

The Planning Policy team publishes the new rules as a PDF document. Meanwhile, Development Management continues to use older spatial layers in their separate IT system. There is no automated connection between the newly adopted rules and the systems used to enforce them daily.

Best Practice: Rules-as-Code API Publishing

Modern architectures align with the MHCLG objective of "Rules-as-code". When a Local Plan is adopted, its spatial constraints (e.g., Conservation Areas, Tree Preservation zones) are published to the corporate data store and instantly exposed via an API. The Development Management "dynamic forms" frontend is hardwired to consume this API, meaning applicants immediately face the new rules the moment the plan is legally adopted.

Real-world impact
  • Service Cohesion

    Closes the critical gap between Policy creation and Dev Control enforcement. It ensures the council acts as a single entity using a single source of truth.

  • National Alignment

    By exposing these policies as structured APIs, the council automatically complies with central government mandates to publish local plan data to planning.data.gov.uk.

6 Monitoring

  • Business Process
  • Anti-patterns
  • Target Architecture

The process: A requirement of local plans is that they include a plan for monitoring the policies and their impact. Currently this means manually counting key statistics every year, placing a significant burden on stretched teams.

Required LGAM Taxonomy Nodes:

Business intelligence and analytics
Anti-pattern: Manual data collection

An officer is required to manually review planning applications or carry out physical site surveys to extract key data points.

Best Practice: Automated and integrated monitoring

If monitoring is built into the planning application workflow, live data can be captured automatically throughout the plan period, reducing manual involvement and increasing the usefulness of the data collected.

Real-world impact
  • Better data insights

    Real-time data with fewer errors gives planners and the wider ecosystem more confidence in how policies are performing.

Target data models

Planning Policy is the primary generator of spatial rules. These outputs must precisely align with MHCLG national schemas so they can be universally understood by the market.

Dataset Schema Architectural Purpose
Local plans The overarching schema for the spatial development strategy. It must be published as structured data, not just text, defining exact geographic boundaries. View the dataset definition.
Brownfield land Statutory register of previously developed land. Maintaining this as a live, API-accessible schema rather than an annual CSV export ensures continuous compliance.
Timetable data There is a statutory requirement for plan-making autorities to publish their local plan timetable in a standardised format, this must be updated at key points in the process.

What makes planning policy technically different

Every council domain has integration points with shared capabilities. Planning policy is architecturally distinctive in several ways that affect how you design those integrations:

The problem is the process, not the PDF

Earlier "digital local plans" focused on publishing a more interactive version of the plan document. Research with local planning authorities found the real pain sits in plan-making itself: evidence, policy wording, consultation responses, modifications and maps are held separately in Word, Excel, GIS and the website, and the same information is collated by hand again and again. This means:

  • The plan should be built from a single structured source of truth, with policies, evidence, consultation and spatial data held as linked data rather than separate documents.
  • Website pages, consultation drafts and submission documents should be generated from that source, not maintained as parallel copies.
  • A PDF may still be required, for example by inspectors, but it should be an output generated from the data rather than the master record.

A statutory, multi-year process with fixed gateways

Under the new plan-making system, a local plan follows a 30-month process with defined stages, gateway assessments and an examination by the Planning Inspectorate (PINS). The plan timetable and housing requirement must be published as data. This means:

  • The plan timetable and its milestones should be structured data, ideally recording which regulation each published date satisfies so that compliance can be checked automatically.
  • Submissions to PINS at each gateway and at examination should move towards automated, auditable data exchange rather than manually numbered, printed and emailed document bundles.
  • Data captured at each stage should follow MHCLG's published planning data standards rather than a local data model.

Version history is a core requirement

Policy wording changes many times through consultation, examination and modifications. Today this is tracked with tracked changes and multiple copies of the same document. Developers, agents and decision makers need to know which version of a policy applied at a given date, and why it changed. This means:

  • Each policy should be versioned as data, with the reason for each change recorded, for example a main or minor modification proposed at examination.
  • Differences between versions should be generated automatically rather than produced by hand.
  • The status of every policy document (emerging, submitted, adopted or superseded) should be clear, and people should be able to be notified when a policy that affects them changes.

Policies only make sense alongside their evidence

Inspectors, development management officers and consultants all need to understand where a policy came from. Preparing for examination currently means manually reviewing large volumes of evidence and consultation responses for each inspector question. This means:

  • Policies need explicit links to the evidence base, consultation responses and the national policy (such as the NPPF) that informed them.
  • Consultation responses should be structured by theme, policy and respondent so officers can respond consistently and in bulk.
  • Inspectors' questions should be linkable to the relevant policies, evidence and responses, so examination preparation can be partly automated.

Spatial data is part of the policy

The policies map, site allocations and constraint layers are a legal part of the plan, not an illustration of it. Statutory consultees rely on spatial data but still receive it manually, and planners often want to start from the map. This means:

  • Every policy should have a geospatial representation, even where it applies to the whole plan area.
  • Policy layers should follow MHCLG's guidance on presenting the policies map and be shared as reliable, reusable data.
  • GIS integration needs to work both ways, because modifications can change policy boundaries during examination.

Part of a wider, changing ecosystem

Plan-making depends on tools and services outside the policy team: call for sites, digital consultation, PINS submission, and national services being developed by MHCLG. Local policy also sits within a hierarchy of national policy and, outside London, new SDSs, while local government reorganisation will change which bodies make plans. This means:

  • A plan-making system must interoperate through open APIs with consultation, call for sites, GIS and PINS services rather than replacing them.
  • The data structure should be modular and authority-agnostic so it can absorb regulatory change and scale to other policy documents such as SDSs.
  • Policy hierarchy matters: users need to see local, strategic and national policy that applies to a site together.
